Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J35/J35nB336.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huigongxiong of Baoxianglin, Nanhai. Huigong Kaixiong raises an unnamed monk asking Touzi Yiqing whose song he sings and whose line he inherits. Touzi gives an arrow before the primordial Buddha piercing two mountains; asked about what is transmitted, he answers with the moon of Huai lighting the spring of Ying. The monk's comparison with seeing a tall person in water draws Touzi's rebuke that he knows precious jade's rarity but not the king's heart, followed by a whisk strike. Huigong praises the exchange's immense force, then asks who made that arrow. The headword is Touzi's inherited answer, while Huigong turns its image into another present question.

Guantao Daqi recounts Touzi's answer about the Huai moon illuminating Ying's spring, the monk's attempted acknowledgment and Touzi's rebuke and whisk strike. Guantao calls Touzi an outstanding figure who opens territory and renews the old, but asks where his single arrow has landed now. Anyone who can say may travel freely throughout the world. The exact headword belongs to Touzi, not Guantao's own reply to a new monk. Its moon-and-spring image figures transmission, while the current question prevents treating transmission as completed merely by repeating that image or naming the inherited line.

Zhe'an Jingfan raises the same lineage exchange: Touzi's primordial arrow, the Huai moon lighting Ying's spring and his rebuke of the monk who thinks he has recognized the answer. Zhe'an praises Touzi for carrying forward the old enterprise as vigorously as Bodhidharma, but worries that the monk has accepted the transmitted matter crudely, without transformation. He says he cannot untangle it tonight and will explain tomorrow. The headword remains Touzi's quoted answer; the later teacher's postponement and doubt keep the monk's acknowledgment open to scrutiny rather than certifying it as full realization.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB392.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Hansong Cao. Hansong Zhicao includes Touzi as the seventeenth generation in a succession account. After the moon-and-spring answer and the monk's acknowledgment, this recension has Touzi strike the incense stand with his whisk, rather than explicitly strike the monk. Hansong's verse praises one arrow penetrating towering barriers, then gives the Huai moon leaving spring at Ying and flowers of Caoxi blooming on Tongxi's tree. Senses.Explanation: To present in full is to bring the whole matter forward without leaving a remainder; the phrase appears in questions, answers, and appraisals of complete presentation. Literally, to raise or present in full. Yunmen Wenyan supplies the decisive contrast: seeing no single form is only half-presentation, and even then one must know the occasion of full presentation. Shengyin Chongkai pairs presentation across past and present with the ancestral master's true command. Juelang Dasheng joins the flower at Vulture Peak and snow at Shaoshi with separate transmission personally shown and the true command fully presented. Yuanwu Keqin raises the command in full and publicly asks how it can be unfolded. Liao'an Qingyu says that the entrustment at Vulture Peak is precisely here and tells the assembly to take up one fully presented saying; Shending Yunwai Ze similarly says that if one can present it whole with bare hands, ease is assured. Zen bends the ordinary sense of completeness toward teaching-seat language: a saying, command, or lineage entrustment is brought forward without remainder and submitted to the assembly.

Senses.Explanation: The whole body stands exposed means that the complete thing is already openly displayed, even where the person facing it fails to recognize it. Wuwai Wunian Yuanxin gives the contrast in one exchange: face-to-face it is not recognized, yet its whole body stands openly exposed. Miyun Wuyun likewise places the phrase in broad daylight under a clear sky after refusing both talk and silence as resting places. The exposed whole is not restricted to a human body. Ruibai Mingxue uses one jewel whose full body is present through its colored reflections; Puan Yinsu uses one broken grain of ordinary Luling rice; Jifei Ruyi answers from within the ocean-seal’s light. These images make exposure observable through what is present rather than through a hidden explanation. Failure to recognize it and differences among reflected colors do not make the whole absent. Body, jewel, grain, and luminous field are distinct images carrying one recurrent predicate: the complete referent is out in the open. They are not four separate dictionary senses.

Senses.Explanation: “Walking alone in the cinnabar sky” is a high, solitary stride used for someone who clears a presented condition or stands beyond the surrounding company. Mingjue Cong, Hanxiu, Tianran Hanshi, and Guxue Zhe connect it with understanding a four-line arrangement, completing a summer period, escaping a verbal impasse, or finding a way out. Mingjue Cong says that understanding host, guest, illumination, and function permits the solitary stride. Hanxiu pairs it with sitting atop Vairocana and standing beyond things. Tianran Hanshi asks how someone unable to answer can walk there; Guxue Zhe promises the stride if the assembly can state a way out.

Senses.Explanation: A token of trust is an object presented or retained as evidence of acknowledgment or transmission, especially a robe, staff, or whisk. Feiyin Tongrong raises the robe and asks how trust can be shown after saying masters use it as a token. Miyun Yuanwu says the ancestral robe was transmitted as such a token and contrasts it with his own present verification. The Huineng-Huiming case calls the robe a token not worth fighting over. Later instructions entrust a whisk or staff to a student as a token to be kept and eventually brought out.
